input:
## Case

This proposal concerns the construction of a water recycling plant for the site. At present, the site takes all of its water from an external supply and discharges all of its effluent after treatment. It is worth noting that a significant part of the site's water demand consists of uses that do not actually require fresh-water quality, such as washdown and utility make-up, and these uses currently draw on the incoming supply simply because no alternative source has been connected to them. The proposed recycling plant would take a suitable effluent stream after treatment, treat it further to the quality that those uses require, and return it to them, thereby meeting part of the site's demand from water that the site has already used once.

The case for the plant rests on the overall structure of the site's water flows. Every unit of water that is recycled is a unit that does not have to be purchased from the external supply, and it is also a unit that does not have to be discharged, so the plant has an effect at both ends of the site's water position at the same time. A site that recycles part of its flow is less exposed to interruption or restriction in the external supply, and also less exposed to any tightening of the conditions on its discharge, than a site that passes the whole of its demand through the boundary in both directions. Furthermore, the recycled flow is under the site's own control, and its availability follows the site's own operation rather than a supplier's network.

The scope of the proposal is the site's own uses. The plant would not supply water to third parties, and it would not replace the existing effluent treatment, since the residual stream that is not recycled would continue to that treatment and to discharge as at present. The plant should be seen as an addition between the treated effluent and the low-grade uses, and its sizing would follow those uses rather than the whole of the site's demand. Uses that need fresh-water quality would remain on the external supply.

The alternative to the plant is simply to continue with the present arrangement, under which the low-grade uses remain on purchased water and the treated effluent continues to be discharged in full. That arrangement works, although it does not give the site any reduction in its exposure on either side. Partial measures short of the plant, such as returning untreated or partly treated water to the least demanding uses, have been set aside on quality grounds, because the receiving uses still have quality requirements that have to be met.

It should also be emphasised that the boundary between the recycled supply and the fresh supply is an important feature of the proposal. The recycled supply would be carried in separate pipework, and the design would include arrangements for monitoring its quality and for diverting it back to treatment if it were found to be off specification, so that it could not reach a use for which it was not intended.

## Costs

The capital cost of the plant is $2351k. This figure covers the plant as a whole, including the treatment equipment, the storage, the pipework and tie-ins to the effluent stream and to the receiving uses, the installation, and the commissioning. No breakdown of the figure between these elements is provided at this stage, because such a breakdown is a product of the detailed design, and presenting one now would suggest a level of precision that the underlying design does not yet support.

The appraisal horizon is 7 years. Within that horizon, the operating costs of the plant are to be set against its savings. The operating costs are the running costs of the treatment itself, including energy, treatment chemicals, operating labour, maintenance of the plant and its instruments, and the cost of the residual discharge that remains. The savings are the purchased water that would no longer be bought for the uses the plant supplies, and the discharge charges that would no longer be paid on the recycled flow. Neither side of this running account is quantified in this proposal, because the quantities follow from the detailed design and from the operating pattern of the receiving uses, and both will be reported when the design is complete. The capital figure is therefore the cost figure on which this proposal asks for a decision, and the decision it supports is the decision to design, rather than the decision to build.

## Schedule

The schedule starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design, which will confirm the effluent streams that the plant draws on, the quality that the receiving uses require, the treatment route, and the sizing of the plant against the demand pattern of the uses it will serve. The design stage will also fix the tie-in points, the storage between treatment and use, and the control arrangements.

Procurement and construction will follow the design, and they will be subject to a separate approval. It should be noted that no contractor is named in this proposal, and no construction commitment is sought at this stage. The construction schedule is itself an output of the design stage, because the duration of the build will follow from the plant that the design specifies and from the windows that the site can offer for tie-ins to live systems. The tie-ins represent the principal constraint on the schedule, since the effluent stream and the receiving uses are in service, and the connection points will have to be taken when the site can release them.

## Decision requested

The decision that is requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. It is not approval to construct, and nothing in this proposal commits the site to the build itself. The product of the design stage will be the material that the construction decision needs, namely a firmer capital cost in place of the proposal figure of $2351k, an operating account that is quantified on both sides, a construction schedule set against the site's tie-in windows, and the treatment route and sizing fixed in engineering detail.

Approving the design stage would buy that material at design cost while holding every later commitment open. Declining it would leave the site on its present arrangement. If the design stage returns figures that no longer support the case, the proposal will end at that point and the construction decision will never be reached, which is the reason for staging the decision in this way.

## Case

The proposal covers a water recycling plant for the site. The site takes its water from an external supply and discharges its effluent after treatment. Between the two flows sit uses that do not need fresh-water quality: washdown, utility make-up and similar services that at present draw on the incoming supply because no other source is connected to them. The recycling plant takes a suitable effluent stream after treatment, brings it to the quality those uses require, and returns it to them, so that part of the site's demand is met from water the site has already used once.

The case rests on the structure of the site's water flows rather than on any single figure. Every unit of water recycled is a unit not purchased from the external supply and a unit not discharged, so the plant acts on both ends of the site's water position at once. A site that recycles part of its flow is less exposed to interruption or restriction in the external supply, and less exposed to tightening of the conditions on its discharge, than a site that passes the whole of its demand through the boundary in both directions. The plant also changes what the site has to plan around: the recycled flow is under the site's own control, available whenever the effluent stream it draws on is running, and its availability follows the site's operation rather than a supplier's network.

The quality boundary deserves a statement of its own, because it is the feature on which the plant's safety case rests. A recycled supply is a second water system on the site, running alongside the fresh supply, and the two are kept apart by design: separate pipework, marked at every point where the two systems come near each other, and no cross-connection through which recycled water could reach a use that needs fresh quality. The design stage fixes the quality the recycled supply is treated to, the monitoring that proves the quality continuously, and the diversion that sends an off-specification supply back to treatment rather than forward to the uses. A recycling plant whose product quality is not controlled in that way transfers a water problem into the equipment it feeds, and the proposal does not contemplate one.

The scope is the site's own uses. The plant supplies no water to third parties, and it does not replace the existing effluent treatment: the residual stream that is not recycled continues to that treatment and to discharge as now. The plant is an addition between the treated effluent and the low-grade uses, and its sizing follows those uses, not the whole of the site's demand. Uses that need fresh-water quality stay on the external supply, and the boundary between the two supplies is fixed by the quality each use requires, not by convenience of pipework.

The alternative to the plant is the present arrangement continued: the low-grade uses stay on purchased water, and the treated effluent continues to discharge in full. That arrangement works, and its costs are the running costs of purchase and discharge; what it does not give the site is any reduction in its exposure on either side. Partial measures short of the plant, such as returning untreated or partly treated water to the least demanding uses, were set aside on quality grounds: the receiving uses still have quality requirements, and a supply that is not controlled to those requirements risks the equipment it feeds. The plant as proposed is the smallest step that puts the recycled supply under treatment and control.

## Costs

The capital cost of the plant is $2351k. The figure covers the plant as a whole: treatment equipment, storage, pipework and tie-ins to the effluent stream and to the receiving uses, installation, and commissioning. No split of the figure between those elements is given at this stage; the split is a product of the detailed design, and presenting one now would give the appraisal a precision the underlying design does not yet have.

The appraisal horizon is 7 years. Within that horizon the plant's operating costs stand against its savings. The operating costs are the running costs of the treatment itself: energy, treatment chemicals, operating labour, maintenance of the plant and its instruments, and the cost of the residual discharge that remains. The savings are the purchased water no longer bought for the uses the plant supplies and the discharge charges no longer paid on the recycled flow. Neither side of that running account is quantified in this proposal: the quantities follow from the detailed design's sizing and from the operating pattern of the receiving uses, and both are reported when the design is complete. The capital figure is therefore the cost figure on which this proposal asks for a decision, and the decision it supports is the decision to design, not yet the decision to build.

Two features of the capital figure should be held in mind while it is used. The figure is a proposal-stage figure, built from the plant's duty and from comparable installations rather than from a priced design, and its accuracy is the accuracy of that stage: it is firm enough to decide whether the design is worth buying, and not firm enough to commit construction funds. It is also a figure for the plant as scoped above; a change in the receiving uses, in the quality boundary, or in the effluent streams available to draw on is a change in the plant, and the figure moves with it. The design stage reports the figure again with its basis, so that the construction decision can see what the number rests on and what would move it.

## Schedule

The schedule starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design: confirmation of the effluent streams the plant draws on, the quality the receiving uses require, the treatment route that closes the distance between the two, and the sizing of the plant against the demand pattern of the uses it will serve. The design stage also fixes the tie-in points, the storage between treatment and use, and the control that keeps a recycled supply of off-specification quality out of the receiving systems.

Procurement and construction follow the design, and they are subject to a separate approval: no contractor is named in this proposal, and no construction commitment is sought at this stage. The construction schedule is itself an output of the design stage, since the duration of the build follows from the plant the design specifies and from the windows the site can offer for tie-ins to live systems. Tie-ins are the schedule's constraint: the effluent stream and the receiving uses are in service, and the points at which the plant connects to them have to be taken when the site can release them. The design stage identifies those windows and builds the construction sequence around them, so the schedule that returns for the construction decision is a schedule against stated windows rather than a duration asserted in advance.

## Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. It is not approval to construct, and nothing in this proposal commits the site to the build. The product of the design stage is the material the construction decision needs: a firmer capital cost in place of the proposal figure of $2351k, an operating account quantified on both sides, a construction schedule set against the site's tie-in windows, and the treatment route and sizing fixed in engineering detail.

The design stage is also the point at which the proposal's open items are closed out in engineering terms: the treatment route is selected against the measured quality of the effluent streams, the storage is sized against the pattern of demand rather than its average, and the control and diversion arrangements are specified to the standard the quality boundary requires. None of that work commits the site beyond the design fee, and all of it is reusable in a revised proposal if the construction decision goes against this one.

Approving the design stage buys that material at design cost and holds every later commitment open. Declining it leaves the site on its present arrangement, with the case above standing as the record of what was considered. If the design stage returns figures that no longer support the case, the proposal ends there, and the construction decision is never reached; that is the point of staging the decision in this way.
